property_summary: For any caller who is the current owner, calling transferOwnership(newOwner) updates the contract's public owner to newOwner; the mutant that removes the assignment fails this rule for inputs where the caller is the owner and newOwner != original owner.

For any address newOwner and any address caller that is the current owner, calling transferOwnership(newOwner) results in c.owner() == newOwner afterwards; the mutant that omits assignment breaks this when caller is the current owner and newOwner != original owner.

For every admissible pair (currentOwnerCaller, newOwner) where currentOwnerCaller is the contract's initial owner, calling transferOwnership(newOwner) results in c.owner() == newOwner; the mutant that omits the assignment can violate this (owner remains unchanged) for some fuzzed newOwner.

For any address newOwner (not equal to the initial owner), when the initial owner calls transferOwnership(newOwner) the contract's public owner becomes newOwner; the mutant that removes the assignment can violate this (owner stays the original) for some fuzzed newOwner.

For any caller that is the current owner and any non-zero new owner address, calling transferOwnership(_newOwner) results in c.owner() == _newOwner; the mutant that sets owner = address(0) violates this when _newOwner != address(0).

For any caller who is the current owner, transferring ownership to a new address sets c.owner() to that provided new address; the mutant that assigns owner = address(0) breaks this (when the provided _newOwner != address(0)).

For any caller that is the current owner and any new owner address, after transferOwnership(newOwner) completes the contract's public owner() equals the provided newOwner; the mutant that sets owner = address(0) breaks this when newOwner != address(0).

For any caller who is the current owner and any address _newOwner, after calling transferOwnership(_newOwner) the contract's owner() equals the supplied _newOwner; the mutant that assigns owner = msg.sender breaks this because owner() remains the caller instead of _newOwner for some inputs.

For any caller who is the current owner, calling transferOwnership(newOwner) sets owner() to the supplied newOwner; the mutant that assigns owner = msg.sender breaks this because after the call owner() remains the caller instead of the provided newOwner for some (fuzzed) newOwner addresses.

For any address newOwner and any caller who is the current owner, after calling transferOwnership(newOwner) the contract's owner() equals the supplied newOwner; the mutant that sets owner = msg.sender leaves owner() equal to the caller for some fuzzed newOwner inputs, violating this rule.

For any nonzero address newOwner and when the caller is the current owner, calling transferOwnership(newOwner) results in c.owner() == newOwner; the mutant that assigns owner = msg.sender instead leaves owner() == caller for some fuzzed newOwner, so the property is violated.

For any address newOwner and when the caller is the current owner, after calling transferOwnership(newOwner) the contract's owner() equals the supplied newOwner; the mutant that assigns owner = msg.sender leaves owner() equal to the caller for some fuzzed newOwner addresses, violating this rule.

For every caller and newOwner value, the reference contract ensures only the current owner can change owner via transferOwnership; the mutant removing the require allows some callers (non-owners) to change owner, breaking that invariant.

For every caller and newOwner input, only the current owner can successfully call transferOwnership and change C.owner(); the mutant inverts the modifier allowing non-owners to perform the transfer and thus can change owner when the caller is not the current owner.

For any caller address x and newOwner address y, only a current owner can successfully call transferOwnership — after calling transferOwnership as msg.sender x, C.owner() == x if and only if the call succeeded; the mutant inverts the owner check allowing non-owners to change owner, so there exist x,y where a non-owner call changes owner.

For any caller who is the current owner and any newOwner address, calling transferOwnership(newOwner) updates C.owner() to equal newOwner; the mutant that assigns owner = owner breaks this by leaving owner unchanged for some newOwner values.

For any caller who is the current owner, calling transferOwnership(newOwner) sets C.owner() to newOwner (the mutant that assigns owner = owner can leave owner unchanged, so there exists a newOwner for which the mutant's owner() != newOwner while the reference always sets owner() == newOwner).

For any caller who is the current owner and any newOwner address, calling transferOwnership(newOwner) results in c.owner() == newOwner (the mutant that assigns owner = owner can leave owner unchanged so for some newOwner the mutant's owner() != newOwner).

For any address newOwner and when the caller is the current owner, calling transferOwnership(newOwner) updates the contract's public owner() to exactly newOwner; the mutant that does owner = owner can leave owner unchanged, violating this property for inputs where newOwner != previous owner.

For any address newOwner and when the caller is the current owner, calling transferOwnership(newOwner) results in c.owner() equaling newOwner; the mutant that does owner = owner can leave owner unchanged, so there exist inputs where the mutant's owner() != newOwner.

For any caller who is the contract's current owner, calling transferOwnership(newOwner) updates the owner to the provided newOwner (i.e., owner becomes the call's _newOwner); the mutant that first sets _newOwner = owner breaks this by leaving owner unchanged for some fuzzed newOwner inputs.

For any caller that is the contract owner, calling owned() does not change the owner; the buggy mutant assigns owner = address(0) inside owned(), violating this invariant for some owner caller addresses.

For any caller who is the contract owner, invoking owned() must preserve the owner state (owner remains equal to the caller); the mutant breaks this by setting owner = address(0) inside owned(), making owner != caller after the call for the owner caller input.

For any caller, calling owned() as set up in the reference C does not change the owner (owner remains the same); the mutant that assigns owner = msg.sender inside owned() can change owner when owned() is callable by a non-owner (e.g., if onlyOwner is bypassed), so the mutant can result in owner != original owner for some inputs.

Calling owned() never changes the stored owner in the correct contract (owner remains equal to the pre-call owner for every caller); the mutant that assigns owner = msg.sender inside owned() can change owner when owned() becomes callable by a non-owner, so there exist inputs where owner after the call != owner before the call.

Calling owned() does not change the contract's owner for any caller when the onlyOwner modifier is enforced; the mutant that assigns owner = msg.sender inside owned() would allow owner to change if owned() is ever callable by a non-owner, so there exist inputs (a caller address) that make owner after the call differ from owner before the call.

For every caller address, invoking owned() does not change C.owner (owner after call equals owner before call); the mutant that assigns owner = msg.sender inside owned() can cause owner to change for some caller, so the property will fail for that mutant.

For any caller address, invoking owned() does not change C.owner (owner remains equal to its pre-call value); the mutant that assigns owner = msg.sender inside owned() can make owner differ after the call for some caller, so the property fails on that mutant.

The owner state is immutable to calls to owned() by non-owners: in the reference, only the current owner can execute owned(), so calling owned() never changes owner when invoked by a non-owner; the mutant removes the require and therefore allows a non-owner invocation of owned() to change owner for some inputs.

For every caller address, calling owned() does not change the contract's owner unless the caller is the current owner; the mutant removes the onlyOwner check so some non-owner caller can call owned() and change owner, violating this invariant.

Invariant: calling owned() must not change owner when the caller is not the current owner; the mutant removes the onlyOwner check so a non-owner caller can call owned() and (via a crafted calldata that performs a delegatecall-style state write if owned were writable) change owner — we instead target that only the current owner can successfully call transferOwnership to change owner, so any call to transferOwnership by a non-owner must not change c.owner(); the mutant allowing non-owner execution of owner-only functions would permit a non-owner to change owner via transferOwnership and thus break this rule.

For any caller address, the reference contract only allows the current owner to call owner-restricted functions (calls to owned() succeed for the owner and fail for non-owners); the mutant inverts the check allowing non-owners and thus will allow some non-owner caller to succeed while the reference would reject them (or vice-versa), breaking this access-control rule.
